properties.name: Apollo 11 Lunar Module descent stage
properties.why_left: The descent stage served as the launch platform for the ascent stage, which carried the crew back to the orbiting Command/Service Module. The descent stage was left behind on the Moon.
properties.science_enabled: Its storage bay carried the Early Apollo Scientific Experiment Package (passive seismometer, lunar dust detector) and a laser ranging retroreflector the crew left on the surface. The crew collected 21.55 kg of lunar samples.
properties.current_status: Inactive hardware left on the surface by the crew.

properties.name: Apollo 12 Lunar Module descent stage
properties.why_left: The descent stage served as the launch platform for the ascent stage, which carried the crew back to the orbiting Command/Service Module. The descent stage was left behind on the Moon.
properties.science_enabled: Carried the ALSEP instrument package (passive seismometer, suprathermal ion detector, cold cathode ion gauge, dust detector, magnetometer, solar wind spectrometer). The crew collected 34.35 kg of samples and returned about 10 kg of parts from Surveyor 3, which landed within about 180 m.
properties.current_status: Inactive hardware left on the surface by the crew.

properties.name: Apollo 14 Lunar Module descent stage
properties.why_left: The descent stage served as the launch platform for the ascent stage, which carried the crew back to the orbiting Command/Service Module. The descent stage was left behind on the Moon.
properties.science_enabled: Carried the ALSEP instrument package (passive and active seismometers, suprathermal ion detector, charged particle experiment, cold cathode ion gauge, dust detector). The crew collected 42.28 kg of lunar samples.
properties.current_status: Inactive hardware left on the surface by the crew.

properties.name: Apollo 15 Lunar Module descent stage
properties.why_left: The descent stage served as the launch platform for the ascent stage, which carried the crew back to the orbiting Command/Service Module. The descent stage was left behind on the Moon.
properties.science_enabled: Carried the Lunar Roving Vehicle and the ALSEP package (passive seismometer, magnetometer, solar wind spectrometer, suprathermal ion detector, cold cathode ion gauge, dust detector, heat flow experiment). The crew drove 27.9 km and collected 77.31 kg of samples.
properties.current_status: Inactive hardware left on the surface by the crew.

properties.name: Apollo 16 Lunar Module descent stage
properties.why_left: The descent stage served as the launch platform for the ascent stage, which carried the crew back to the orbiting Command/Service Module. The descent stage was left behind on the Moon.
properties.science_enabled: Carried the Lunar Roving Vehicle and the ALSEP package (passive and active seismometers, magnetometer, heat flow experiment, which was damaged during setup). The crew covered 27 km and collected 95.71 kg of samples.
properties.current_status: Inactive hardware left on the surface by the crew.

properties.name: Apollo 17 Lunar Module descent stage
properties.why_left: The descent stage served as the launch platform for the ascent stage, which carried the crew back to the orbiting Command/Service Module. The descent stage was left behind on the Moon.
properties.science_enabled: Carried the Lunar Roving Vehicle and the ALSEP package (heat flow experiment, surface gravimeter, mass spectrometer, seismic profiling, ejecta and meteorites experiment). The crew covered 30 km and collected 110.52 kg of samples.
properties.current_status: Inactive hardware left on the surface by the crew.

properties.name: Apollo 15 Lunar Roving Vehicle
properties.why_left: The Lunar Roving Vehicle was left on the Moon because only the Lunar Module ascent stage returned to lunar orbit. The rover remained at the Apollo 15 Hadley-Apennine landing site after the astronauts completed their final EVA.
properties.science_enabled: No. The Apollo 15 LRV was a crewed exploration vehicle used for transportation, geological exploration, and astronaut mobility. It did not carry independent long-term science instruments after abandonment.
properties.current_status: Inactive hardware left on the surface by the crew.

properties.name: Surveyor 3 lander (Appx)
properties.why_left: Surveyor 3 was a fixed robotic lander with no way to leave the Moon, so it stayed where it landed in 1967. Apollo 12 landed within about 180 m of it. On 20 November 1969 astronauts Pete Conrad and Alan Bean examined it and removed about 10 kg of parts, including the TV camera. The rest of the spacecraft was left behind.
properties.science_enabled: Its television camera sent close-up images of the lunar surface to check whether the terrain was safe for crewed landings. Its soil mechanics surface sampler scoop dug trenches for soil tests. The parts Apollo 12 brought back were examined on Earth, and the camera is now on display at the Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum.
properties.current_status: Not communicating; no active mission operations.

properties.name: Surveyor 1 lander
properties.last_contact: 1967-01-07 (last engineering interrogation; picture mission ended 1966-07-13 07:30 UT)
properties.why_left: Surveyor 1 was a one-way lander and stayed where it landed. Its picture mission ended on 13 July 1966, after battery voltage dropped sharply just after sunset. Engineering contacts continued until 7 January 1967.
properties.science_enabled: Returned 11,240 pictures of its footpad and the surrounding terrain, plus data on the radar reflectivity and bearing strength of the lunar surface and on spacecraft temperatures. It was the first US spacecraft to land safely on the Moon.
properties.image_credit: NASA (generic Surveyor spacecraft image, via NSSDCA; not a photo of the Surveyor 1 site)
properties.current_status: Not communicating; no active mission operations.

properties.name: Surveyor 5 lander
properties.why_left: Surveyor 5 was a one-way lander and stayed where it landed. Its final transmission came at 04:30 UT on 17 December 1967, after four lunar days of operation.
properties.science_enabled: Returned 19,118 pictures. Its alpha-scattering instrument made the first in-situ chemical analysis of another world's surface, finding soil like basalt. A vernier engine erosion test showed minor erosion of the surface.
properties.current_status: Not communicating; no active mission operations.

properties.name: Surveyor 6 lander
properties.why_left: Surveyor 6 was a one-way lander. After its hop of about 2.4 m on 17 November 1967 it stayed where it came down. It was put into hibernation for the lunar night, and the last transmission came on 14 December 1967 with no useful data.
properties.science_enabled: Returned 29,952 images and 30 hours of alpha-scattering data showing a basaltic surface. On 17 November 1967 it made the first powered takeoff from the lunar surface, a 3 to 4 m hop that gave stereo views of the site. Its soil data showed the surface could support human landings.
properties.image_credit: NASA (Surveyor 6 panorama of Sinus Medii, via NSSDCA)
properties.current_status: Not communicating; no active mission operations.

properties.name: Surveyor 7 lander
properties.why_left: Surveyor 7 was a one-way lander and stayed where it landed. Operations ended on 21 February 1968 after two lunar days of work.
properties.science_enabled: Returned 21,038 pictures and 100 hours of alpha-scattering data in all, from the Tycho highlands. Its surface sampler dug trenches and moved four rocks over 36 hours. The highland soil was poorer in iron-group elements than the mare samples from earlier missions. It also detected laser beams sent from Earth.
properties.image_credit: NASA (Surveyor 7 panorama near Tycho, via NSSDCA)
properties.current_status: Not communicating; no active mission operations.

properties.name: Viking 1 Lander (Thomas Mutch Memorial Station) (Appx)
properties.why_left: The lander is a fixed surface station. It has no way to leave Mars: it kept operating until contact was lost, and it remains where it touched down.
properties.science_enabled: Studied the biology, chemical composition, meteorology, seismology, magnetic properties, appearance and physical properties of the martian surface and atmosphere, with two cameras, a sampler arm, a meteorology boom, a seismometer, a biology experiment and a gas chromatograph mass spectrometer.
properties.current_status: Not communicating; no active mission operations.

properties.name: Viking 2 Lander (Gerald Soffen Memorial Station)
properties.why_left: The lander is a fixed surface station. It has no way to leave Mars: it was turned off when its batteries failed and it remains where it landed.
properties.science_enabled: Studied the biology, chemical composition, meteorology, seismology, magnetic properties, appearance and physical properties of the martian surface and atmosphere, with two cameras, a sampler arm, a meteorology boom, a seismometer, a biology experiment and a gas chromatograph mass spectrometer.
properties.current_status: Not communicating; no active mission operations.

properties.name: Sojourner rover and Mars Pathfinder lander (Appx)
properties.why_left: Both the stationary lander and the Sojourner rover stayed at the Ares Vallis site. Images were taken and experiments run until 27 September 1997, when communications were lost for unknown reasons.
properties.science_enabled: Showed that low-cost landings and rover exploration of Mars were feasible. It returned atmospheric entry data, long-range and close-up surface images, rock and soil composition and material-properties measurements, and weather data from the lander's meteorology station. The lander also relayed the rover's data to Earth.
properties.current_status: Not communicating; no active mission operations.

properties.name: Spirit rover landing site (Columbia Memorial Station)
properties.why_left: Spirit concluded its mission in 2010 and stayed on Mars. It had driven 7.7 km.
properties.science_enabled: Landed in Gusev Crater, a possible former lake. By studying the rock record, Spirit and Opportunity confirmed that water was long standing on the surface of Mars in ancient times.
properties.current_status: Not communicating; no active mission operations.

properties.name: Opportunity rover landing site
properties.why_left: Opportunity's last communication with Earth came on 10 June 2018, while a planet-wide dust storm covered its location. NASA declared the mission complete on 13 February 2019. The rover stayed at its final resting spot, Perseverance Valley, after driving 45.16 km.
properties.science_enabled: Landed in Meridiani Planum, where mineral deposits suggested a wet history. By studying the rock record, Spirit and Opportunity confirmed that water was long standing on the surface of Mars in ancient times.
properties.current_status: Not communicating; no active mission operations.

properties.name: InSight lander
properties.why_left: After two failed attempts to communicate with the lander, the mission was declared over, presumably due to the inability of the solar cell batteries to maintain enough power to run the spacecraft, on 21 December 2022.
properties.science_enabled: Carried SEIS, a six-component seismometer; HP3, a self-penetrating heat-flow probe; and RISE, which used the X-band radio to track the planet's motion precisely. Its TWINS wind and temperature sensors, pressure sensor and magnetometer helped separate environmental signals from seismic ones. It also had two cameras, an infrared radiometer and a small laser retroreflector on the deck.
properties.current_status: Not communicating; no active mission operations.

properties.name: Phoenix lander (Appx)
properties.why_left: Phoenix could not leave Mars. As the northern summer ended, the mission had less solar energy to operate. It made its last transmission on 2 November 2008, before its power ran out.
properties.science_enabled: Studied the polar climate, weather and lower atmosphere, and the geomorphology and near-surface regolith of the northern plains, focusing on the role of water. Its instruments were a microscopy, electrochemistry and conductivity analyzer, a robotic arm camera, a surface stereo imager, a thermal and evolved gas analyzer, and a weather station. NASA said in July 2008 that it had confirmed Martian water, which is a press-release headline on the page, so read the release before you quote it.
properties.current_status: Not communicating; no active mission operations.

properties.name: Ranger 7 impact site
properties.why_left: Ranger 7 was designed to fly into the Moon on an impact trajectory and send photographs until impact. It crashed at 2.62 km/s in Mare Cognitum, so the wreck remains there.
properties.science_enabled: Its six TV cameras sent 4,308 photographs of excellent quality during the last 17 minutes of flight. The final image before impact has a resolution of 0.5 m.
properties.image_credit: NASA (image of the Ranger 7 spacecraft, via NSSDCA)
properties.current_status: Destroyed by planned impact or atmospheric entry.

properties.name: Ranger 8 impact site
properties.why_left: Ranger 8 was designed to fly into the Moon on an impact trajectory and send photographs until impact. It crashed at about 2.68 km/s in Mare Tranquillitatis, so the wreck remains there.
properties.science_enabled: Its six TV cameras sent 7,137 photographs of good quality during the last 23 minutes of flight. The final image before impact has a resolution of 1.5 m. A planned camera re-pointing was cancelled so the cameras could cover more of the surface.
properties.image_credit: NASA (image of a Ranger spacecraft, via NSSDCA)
properties.current_status: Destroyed by planned impact or atmospheric entry.

properties.name: Ranger 9 impact site
properties.why_left: Ranger 9 was designed to fly into the Moon on an impact trajectory and send photographs until impact. It crashed at 2.67 km/s in the crater Alphonsus, so the wreck remains there.
properties.science_enabled: Its six TV cameras sent 5,814 good-contrast photographs during the last 19 minutes of flight. The final image before impact has a resolution of 0.3 m. Many of the pictures were broadcast live on network television.
properties.image_credit: NASA (image of a Ranger spacecraft, via NSSDCA)
properties.current_status: Destroyed by planned impact or atmospheric entry.

properties.name: Lunar Orbiter 1 (Appx)
properties.why_left: The early end to the nominal one year mission was due to the small amount of remaining attitude control gas and other deteriorating conditions and was planned to avoid transmission interference with Lunar Orbiter 2.
properties.science_enabled: Detailed lunar surface mapping, geological study, Apollo landing-site selection, and measurements of the Moon’s radiation and micrometeoroid environment.
properties.image_credit: NASA (image of a Ranger spacecraft, via NSSDCA)
properties.hardware: Orbiter, ended by impact or atmospheric entry
properties.current_status: Destroyed by planned impact or atmospheric entry.

properties.name: Lunar Orbiter 2 (Appx)
properties.why_left: Commanded to impact the Moon after completing its mission and tracking operations.
properties.science_enabled: High-resolution lunar surface mapping, detailed geological study of craters and terrain, Apollo landing-site evaluation, and micrometeoroid environment measurements.
properties.image_credit: NASA (image of a Ranger spacecraft, via NSSDCA)
properties.hardware: Orbiter, ended by impact or atmospheric entry
properties.current_status: Destroyed by planned impact or atmospheric entry.

properties.name: Lunar Orbiter 3 (Appx)
properties.why_left: Commanded to impact the Moon after completing its photography and tracking mission.
properties.science_enabled: High-resolution lunar mapping, safe landing-site confirmation for Surveyor and Apollo, identification of the Surveyor 1 landing site, and measurements of lunar radiation and micrometeoroid impacts.
properties.image_credit: NASA (image of a Ranger spacecraft, via NSSDCA)
properties.hardware: Orbiter, ended by impact or atmospheric entry
properties.current_status: Destroyed by planned impact or atmospheric entry.

properties.name: Lunar Orbiter 4 presumed impact
properties.why_left: Lost contact on 17 July 1967; its orbit naturally decayed and it presumably impacted the Moon by October 31, 1967
properties.science_enabled: Systematic mapping of 99% of the Moon’s near side, geological study of lunar surface features, and measurements of lunar radiation and micrometeoroid impacts.
properties.image_credit: NASA (image of a Ranger spacecraft, via NSSDCA)
properties.last_known_location: Impacted the Moon in 1967; the impact location is unknown.
properties.hardware: Orbiter, ended by impact or atmospheric entry
properties.current_status: Destroyed by planned impact or atmospheric entry.

properties.name: Lunar Orbiter 5 (Appx)
properties.why_left: Commanded to impact the Moon after completing its photography, experiments, and tracking mission.
properties.science_enabled: Additional Apollo and Surveyor landing-site photography, mapping of previously unphotographed lunar regions, and measurements of lunar radiation and micrometeoroid impacts.
properties.image_credit: NASA (image of a Ranger spacecraft, via NSSDCA)
properties.hardware: Orbiter, ended by impact or atmospheric entry
properties.current_status: Destroyed by planned impact or atmospheric entry.

properties.name: Grail A
properties.why_left: Mission ended after completing the lunar gravity-mapping science phase; spacecraft was intentionally impacted on the Moon.
properties.science_enabled: Mapping the Moon’s gravity field, crust and lithosphere structure, impact basins and mascons, and constraining its thermal evolution and deep interior.
properties.image_credit: NASA (GRAIL spacecraft illustration; attribution awaiting owner review)
properties.hardware: Orbiter, ended by impact or atmospheric entry
properties.current_status: Destroyed by planned impact or atmospheric entry.

properties.name: Grail B
properties.why_left: Mission ended after completing the lunar gravity-mapping science phase; spacecraft was intentionally impacted on the Moon.
properties.science_enabled: Mapping the Moon’s gravity field, crust and lithosphere structure, impact basins and mascons, and constraining its thermal evolution and deep interior.
properties.image_credit: NASA (GRAIL spacecraft illustration; attribution awaiting owner review)
properties.hardware: Orbiter, ended by impact or atmospheric entry
properties.current_status: Destroyed by planned impact or atmospheric entry.

properties.name: LADEE (eastern rim of Sundman V crater)
properties.why_left: Its science mission ended and the spacecraft was intentionally impacted on the Moon on April 18, 2014 after its low-altitude orbit naturally decayed.
properties.science_enabled: Study of the lunar exosphere’s composition and variability, lunar dust environment, micrometeoroid-generated dust, and the interaction between lunar dust and the atmosphere.
properties.image_credit: NASA (LADEE spacecraft; attribution awaiting owner review)
properties.hardware: Orbiter, ended by impact or atmospheric entry
properties.current_status: Destroyed by planned impact or atmospheric entry.

properties.name: Cassini (Appx)
properties.last_contact: 2017-09-15 (final signal received at Earth about 11:55 UTC).
properties.why_left: Deliberately sent into Saturn as fuel ran low, protecting potentially habitable moons from accidental contamination.
properties.science_enabled: Observed Enceladus’s water-rich plumes and Titan’s methane lakes. These discoveries made ocean moons major targets for later exploration.
properties.last_known_location: Approximate Saturn atmospheric entry at 9.4 degrees north, 53 degrees west; not a solid-surface wreck location.
properties.hardware: Orbiter, ended by impact or atmospheric entry
properties.current_status: Destroyed by planned impact or atmospheric entry.

properties.name: Surveyor 2 (Appx)
properties.last_contact: 1966-09-22 around 09:34 UTC; separate from reported impact date 23 September.
properties.why_left: A failed correction thruster caused an uncontrolled spin; contact ended during descent.
properties.science_enabled: Returned no lunar surface science. The failed descent supplied engineering experience for the continuing Surveyor program.
properties.last_known_location: Historically reported approximate lunar impact area southeast of Copernicus; no located wreck is claimed.
properties.current_status: Not communicating; no active mission operations.

properties.name: Surveyor 4 (Appx)
properties.why_left: Radio stopped during descent; a retro-rocket explosion was suspected, not conclusively established.
properties.science_enabled: No surface pictures or soil measurements were returned. Its loss highlighted descent-system risks for subsequent missions.
properties.last_known_location: Approximate intended descent/impact area at Sinus Medii; NASA lists the actual impact location as unknown.
properties.current_status: Not communicating; no active mission operations.

properties.name: Lunar Prospector (Appx)
properties.why_left: Intentionally crashed into a shadowed south-polar crater after its mapping mission, seeking an observable water signal.
properties.science_enabled: Neutron measurements found polar hydrogen consistent with water ice; gravity and elemental maps improved understanding of the Moon. The impact produced no detected water plume.
properties.hardware: Orbiter, ended by impact or atmospheric entry
properties.current_status: Destroyed by planned impact or atmospheric entry.

properties.name: Mars Polar Lander (Appx)
properties.why_left: Likely crashed after landing-leg signals were mistaken for touchdown and the engines shut down early; the failure was not directly observed.
properties.science_enabled: No surface science returned. The loss led to changes in testing and landing-system design.
properties.last_known_location: Approximate intended landing/search area: 76 degrees south, 195 degrees west (165 degrees east). Actual crash location remains unconfirmed.
properties.current_status: Not communicating; no active mission operations.

properties.name: Apollo 12 ALSEP station (Appx)
properties.last_contact: 1977-09-30 (scientific support ended; carrier signals are not science telemetry).
properties.why_left: NASA ended funded operations and scientific data reception after years of extended service. Passive laser reflectors were separate and were not switched off.
properties.science_enabled: Long-term measurements of moonquakes and the lunar environment helped scientists study the Moon’s interior; archived measurements support later reanalysis.
properties.last_known_location: Approximate Apollo 12 landing area; the science station was deployed separately near the lunar module.
properties.current_status: Routine mission operations ended by command or planned retirement.

properties.name: Apollo 16 ALSEP station
properties.last_contact: 1977-09-30 (ALSEP central station shut down along with the other ALSEP stations)
properties.why_left: The astronauts deployed the ALSEP near the Apollo 16 landing site and left it on the surface when they returned to lunar orbit. Its central station was shut down on 30 September 1977 along with the other ALSEP stations. The heat flow experiment had already been rendered inoperable during setup, when a cable was broken.
properties.science_enabled: Carried a passive seismometer for moonquakes and the crust and interior, an active seismometer for the structure of the local near-surface layers, a lunar surface magnetometer, and a heat flow experiment. The central station was turned on on 21 April 1972 and powered by a SNAP-27 radioisotope generator.
properties.last_known_location: Moon surface, Descartes highlands; ALSEP central station at 8.9754 S, 15.4981 E, near where the lunar module landed (8.9730 S, 15.5002 E).
properties.hardware: ALSEP science station (central station with SNAP-27 radioisotope generator, passive and active seismometers, magnetometer, heat flow experiment)
properties.current_status: Routine mission operations ended by command or planned retirement.

properties.name: Apollo 17 ALSEP station
properties.last_contact: 1977-09-30 (ALSEP central station shut down along with the other ALSEP stations)
properties.why_left: The astronauts deployed the ALSEP near the Apollo 17 landing site and left it on the surface when they returned to lunar orbit. Its central station was shut down on 30 September 1977 along with the other ALSEP stations.
properties.science_enabled: Carried a heat flow experiment, a surface gravimeter, a mass spectrometer for the thin lunar atmosphere, a seismic profiling experiment, and a lunar ejecta and meteorites experiment. The central station was turned on on 12 December 1972 and powered by a SNAP-27 radioisotope generator.
properties.last_known_location: Moon surface, Taurus-Littrow valley; ALSEP central station at 20.1921 N, 30.7649 E, near where the lunar module landed (20.1911 N, 30.7723 E).
properties.hardware: ALSEP science station (central station with SNAP-27 radioisotope generator, heat flow experiment, gravimeter, mass spectrometer, seismic profiling and ejecta experiments)
properties.current_status: Routine mission operations ended by command or planned retirement.
